summary:
Have you ever wondered what it takes to send a spacecraft to another planet? There's a lot more to it than just building a rocket and launching it.

That's why our team, **Always A.S.K.**, created **ORBITAL Mission Control**, a game where anyone can design, build, and launch their own space mission.

Players can explore destinations like Mars, the Moon, asteroids, and Europa. They choose their spacecraft's equipment, manage their budget, and make decisions that affect whether their mission succeeds or fails. They can even play with friends, with each person taking on a different role, just like a real mission team.

We created ORBITAL to address the challenge of making space mission design easier to understand and more exciting, especially for students. Instead of just reading about rockets and spacecraft, players get to experiment, face unexpected problems, learn from their mistakes, and try again.

Our goal is simple: make learning about space fun, interactive, and accessible to everyone. We hope our game inspires more people to explore science, engineering, and the universe around us.
details:
Project Description — ORBITAL Mission Control

Have you ever wondered what it actually takes to send a spacecraft to another planet? It's not as simple as building a rocket and launching it. You have to think about fuel, money, electricity, equipment, and a lot of things that could go wrong. And even if you find these info. it might be a complex and hard to understand especially if you were young.

That's what inspired us to create ORBITAL Mission Control, an interactive space mission game developed by our team, Always A.S.K.

In our game, players get to experience what it's like to plan and manage their own space mission in a fun and interactive way. They can choose to play alone or with friends, with each person taking on a different role, such as engineer, scientist, or mission director.

The first step is choosing a destination. Players can travel to the Moon, Mars, an asteroid, or even Europa, one of Jupiter's moons. Then comes the challenging part: building a spacecraft that can actually complete the mission.

Players have to choose their rocket, engine, power source, communication system, and scientific equipment. But there's a catch: every choice has advantages and disadvantages. A powerful rocket might be too expensive, a fuel-efficient engine might take longer to reach its destination, and solar panels might not generate enough electricity far from the Sun.

Once everything is ready, players can launch their mission. During the journey, they might face unexpected problems and have to make decisions that affect the outcome. At the end, they receive a report showing what went well, what went wrong, and what they could improve.

Our main goal is to make learning about space more interesting. We wanted to create something that doesn't just explain how space missions work, but actually lets people experience the decisions involved. We believe that learning is much more enjoyable when you can experiment, make mistakes, and try again.

To build the game, we used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. HTML helped us create the website, CSS allowed us to design its appearance and animations, and JavaScript made the game interactive. We also used SVG and Canvas for visual elements and browser storage to save mission designs and scores. We referred to NASA resources to help us understand the science behind spacecraft design, propulsion, and planetary conditions.

One thing we wanted to make different was the teamwork aspect. In real space missions, engineers, scientists, and mission directors all have different responsibilities. We tried to bring that idea into our game by letting players divide the work and make decisions together.

While developing ORBITAL, one of our biggest challenges was finding the right balance between scientific accuracy and having fun. We didn't want the game to be so complicated that only someone who studies aerospace engineering could understand it. At the same time, we didn't want to teach incorrect science. That's why we used real scientific principles where possible and simplified some numbers and situations to make the game easier to play.

We also wanted the website to be easy to use, including on mobile devices, so that people could enjoy it without downloading anything or owning expensive equipment.

In the end, we hope ORBITAL helps people, especially students, become more curious about space and understand how much planning, creativity, and teamwork go into a real mission.

We're not trying to turn players into astronauts overnight. We just want them to have fun, learn something new, and maybe become a little more interested in the universe around us.
